Concrete request following the established sealed-result pattern. Tarjan's SCC uses only `order()` and `neighbors()` (out-edges), both on the `Graph` interface — and the request explicitly says to use the `Graph` interface, so this one takes `Graph` (it runs on any implementation; on an undirected graph the SCCs are just its connected components).

Design notes:
- **Result type:** SCC has no failure mode, so the meaningful binary that mirrors the established pattern is **`StronglyConnected`** (the whole graph is a single SCC) vs **`Fragmented`** (multiple SCCs). Both expose a uniform `components()` plus an `isStronglyConnected()` predicate. I'll flag this since it's the one judgment call.
- **Iterative Tarjan** (explicit work-stack, not recursion) to keep the deep-graph robustness the other algorithms have.
- Components: vertices sorted ascending within each; the component list is in Tarjan's natural reverse-topological order (documented).

/** * A small, self-contained library for deciding whether an undirected graph is * bipartite, built around a generic adjacency-list representation. * *

Graph representation is layered so new variants can be added without * touching the algorithms: *

    *
  • {@link bipartite.Graph} is the read-only interface algorithms depend * on;
    • *
  • {@link bipartite.AbstractAdjacencyListGraph} is a generic adjacency-list * base parameterised by an incidence type, leaving "what an edge carries" * and "directed vs. undirected" to subclasses;
    • *
  • {@link bipartite.UndirectedGraph}, {@link bipartite.DirectedGraph}, and * {@link bipartite.WeightedUndirectedGraph} are the concrete * implementations;
    • *
  • {@link bipartite.GraphEdge} (with {@link bipartite.Edge} and * {@link bipartite.WeightedEdge}) is the edge contract, and * {@link bipartite.GraphInputValidator} validates construction inputs.
    • *
* *

Algorithms operate against the {@link bipartite.Graph} interface, so they * run unchanged on every implementation. {@link bipartite.BipartiteChecker} runs * a breadth-first 2-coloring and returns the sealed * {@link bipartite.BipartiteResult} — either the two vertex partitions or an * odd-cycle witness — {@link bipartite.DepthFirstSearch} provides a standard * depth-first traversal, {@link bipartite.TopologicalSort} orders a * {@link bipartite.DirectedGraph} so dependencies precede dependents (returning * the sealed {@link bipartite.TopologicalSortResult} — either the order or a * directed-cycle witness), and {@link bipartite.ShortestPath} runs Dijkstra's * algorithm over a {@link bipartite.WeightedUndirectedGraph} (returning the * sealed {@link bipartite.ShortestPathResult} — either the distance and path or * an unreachable notification). * *

{@link bipartite.Main} provides a runnable demonstration, and * {@link bipartite.BipartiteCheckerTests}, * {@link bipartite.DepthFirstSearchTests}, * {@link bipartite.TopologicalSortTests}, and * {@link bipartite.ShortestPathTests} are dependency-free test harnesses. */ package bipartite;

content.text:
Everything compiles; all five harnesses pass (16 + 7 + 8 + 7 + 8 = 46 cases). The demo shows Tarjan correctly isolating the cycle `{0,1,2}` from `{3}` and `{4}`.

## Summary

I added a `StronglyConnectedComponents` algorithm using Tarjan's algorithm, following the established pattern.

**`StronglyConnectedComponentsResult.java`** — sealed `StronglyConnected(component) | Fragmented(components)`, paralleling the other result types. Both variants expose a uniform `components()` (`List<List<Integer>>`) plus an `isStronglyConnected()` predicate; deeply immutable via defensive copies.

**`StronglyConnectedComponents.java`** — `final class`, stateless instance `compute(Graph)` (same API shape as `check`/`traverse`/`sort`/`compute`):
- **Tarjan's algorithm** — one DFS assigning each vertex a discovery index and low-link, emitting a component when a vertex's low-link equals its index.
- **Iterative** (explicit work-stack with `{vertex, nextNeighborIndex}` frames, child low-link folded into the parent on return) — keeping the deep-graph robustness the other algorithms share.
- Depends only on the **`Graph` interface**, so it runs on every implementation. Components are sorted ascending internally and returned in reverse-topological order of the condensation (documented). O(V+E) time/space, fail-fast null check.

**Structural parity:** sealed result, full Javadoc, and a dedicated `StronglyConnectedComponentsTests` harness (8 cases) in the identical style — cycle-with-tail decomposition, single-cycle/single-vertex strong connectivity, DAG singletons, empty graph, a property check that the components partition all vertices, and (demonstrating the interface point) running on an `UndirectedGraph` where SCCs coincide with connected components. Also updated `Main` and `package-info.java`.

**The one design judgment to flag:** SCC has no failure case, so unlike the other algorithms there's no inherent binary. I made the sealed split `StronglyConnected` (one spanning component) vs `Fragmented` (zero/multiple), which is the genuinely useful distinction for SCC analysis and keeps the sealed type semantically meaningful rather than a single-variant wrapper. If you'd instead prefer a single-variant result that just carries `List<List<Integer>>` (no predicate), that's a trivial simplification — say the word.

One observation after five algorithms on this `Graph` foundation: `TopologicalSort`, `ShortestPath`, and `StronglyConnectedComponents` are all inherently directed-graph operations, and `ShortestPath` plus `WeightedUndirectedGraph` point toward a `WeightedGraph` abstraction. If you're continuing to build this out, extracting `DirectedGraph`/`WeightedGraph` interfaces would let these algorithms express their real input constraints at the type level instead of by convention. Happy to do that consolidation whenever it's useful.
